bollymeter.basis: An audacious, visually ravishing work from Paolo Sorrentino that critics admired more than loved - scoring 79% on RT (87 reviews) and 68 on Metacritic, reflecting genuine division between those seduced by its surrealism and those exhausted by its slow pace.

pull_quotes.text: Lush, often surreal, filled with contradictory characters and backstabbing intrigue - one of the more remarkable television shows in memory.
The Young Pope is a fascinating mess with a puckish sense of humor and an outsized goal - to know the mind of God.

seasons.review_body: Paolo Sorrentino brought his signature operatic cinema style to television with this HBO and Sky Atlantic co-production, resulting in sharp differences in viewer temperament. The Rotten Tomatoes score and review count point to a genuine split in response: some audiences connected with the surrealist visual language and Jude Law's magnetic performance of repressed faith, while others found the pacing lugubrious and the plotting cryptic. The series premiered at the Venice Film Festival, the first TV series in competition, and went on to earn two Emmy nominations. Law’s performance stands out for its near universal impact. What Sorrentino builds is less a traditional drama than a meditation on divine power, loneliness, and institutional corruption.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# The Young Pope S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A Pope tells **Tommaso** that he does not believe in God. The sentence lands inside a confession-like setting, where ritual should contain doubt and discipline it into shape. Instead, the hour lets the claim sit there, ugly, funny, dangerous. Earlier, **Lenny Belardo** fights to make the office stick to his body. By the end, the office has renamed him Pope Pius XIII, and he has become a problem for the office. This premiere works because it treats the papacy as an argument over who gets to define reality.

## The Title Is a Weapon Before It Is a Halo

The episode’s sharpest move is to make Lenny’s authority feel unstable before it feels grand. He is challenged with the bluntest possible negation: he is told he is not the Pope. His reply is just as blunt: “I am the Pope!” That line could have played as triumph. Here, it sounds like a man grabbing a ledge.

The premiere understands that identity becomes more frightening when everyone keeps saying it out loud. “The Pope” does not arrive as settled fact. The phrase is pushed around, denied, reclaimed, then reissued with institutional force. the status shift becomes formal. From that point forward, Lenny is Pope Pius XIII. The name matters because the hour has already made naming into combat.

That is the episode’s best early trick. The papacy enters as a dispute. Lenny wants religious authority affirmed, but the drama keeps staging that desire as contradiction. He serves God and insists he will not forget anyone. He rejects casual closeness and praises formal relationships. He wants the role to become undeniable. The more he says it, the less simple it sounds.

The writing leans into dense ideological dialogue, and that density is the point. Everyone speaks as if doctrine, etiquette, and power are different rooms in the same palace. The risk is that dialogue can feel like chess pieces announcing their moves. The reward is a world where a sentence can function as coronation, threat, and confession.

## Formal Relationships, Dangerous Friendships

The Pope’s warning that friendly relationships are dangerous gives the hour its cold operating manual. Lenny does not simply take office. He defines the terms under which anyone may approach him. Formal relationships create distance, and distance is what power needs while it is still proving itself.

That beat gives the episode a clear character argument. Lenny’s authority is staged, defended, fenced off. The premiere refuses to soften him through easy intimacy. Even the language around service to God carries command inside devotion. When the Pope-to-be declares that he serves God and will not forget anyone, the sentiment has a double edge. Memory can be grace. Memory can also be surveillance.

The pauses matter. Speech-heavy scenes are punctured by noticeable silences, including a long opening silence and later gaps. That rhythm suits the hour’s temperament. The talk arrives thick, then the quiet makes the room feel watched. A show about the Vatican can drown in velvet and Latin mood. This episode uses silence as pressure, making formal spaces feel judicial instead of decorative.

The weakness is visible too. Early ideological dialogue piles up fast. At times, the hour trusts abstraction before it has earned emotional access. The result is magnetic, then slightly airless. The episode wants its language to be a maze. Sometimes it becomes a wall. Still, the formal chill has purpose. This is a premiere about a man choosing distance as his first act of rule.

## Voiello as the Spirit in the Machine

The cardinals’ discussion of the Holy Spirit is the hour’s funniest political swerve. They begin in theology and end in machinery, concluding that the Holy Spirit is another name for **Voiello**. That is a wicked compression of the Vatican the episode wants to build: belief on the surface, management underneath, and everyone aware enough to joke about the gears.

The line works because it does not flatten religion into cynicism. It shows how politics borrows religious vocabulary to make itself sound inevitable. If the Holy Spirit can be translated into Voiello, then divine movement has a secretary, a strategy, and likely a filing system. The episode leaves that as an open loop. What exactly does Vatican leadership believe when it says this? Is it a joke, a confession, or the house style?

**Federico** later reports on written works about “me,” including “The man behind the scenes,” and the title carries the same institutional smell. Behind every public face, the hour keeps suggesting a backstage author. The papacy becomes performance, but the performance is made real by everyone agreeing to behave as if it is real.

That is where the premiere has bite. It asks who benefits when belief is administered. Voiello’s presence, even through reported talk and power chatter, gives the hour a counterweight to Lenny’s self-definition. One man says he is the Pope. The institution quietly asks who made that sentence useful.

## Domen’s Theology of Ownership

**Domen** identifying himself as “One who belongs to God” sounds devotional until the logic pulls it into stranger territory. If he belongs to God, and that relation gets linked to belonging to Domen, piety turns into possession. It is a small beat, but it fits the premiere’s larger obsession: every sacred phrase becomes a power claim when spoken in the right room.

The hour’s absurdity helps its severity. The episode has a taste for theological word games, and some come with a dry comic snap. The writing understands that institutions reveal themselves through the grammar they tolerate. Who belongs to whom? Who speaks for whom? Who gets to rename a person, a title, or even the Holy Spirit?

The premiere is strongest when its wordplay has teeth. Domen’s phrasing is not there merely to sound eccentric. It trains the ear for a world where language produces hierarchy. The same pattern governs Lenny’s papal re-identification. It governs the cardinals’ Voiello joke. It governs Tommaso’s confessional exchange. People keep making claims through definitions, and those definitions keep rearranging the room.

The limitation is that character sometimes feels subordinate to concept. Domen’s beat is intriguing because of what it says about the show’s system, less because of what it reveals emotionally. That is acceptable for a pilot, but it sets a challenge. The season will need flesh under the formulation. The ideas are sharp. The people must keep bleeding.

## The Confession Turns the Crown Inside Out

The confession-like scene with Tommaso is the premiere’s boldest closing turn because it attacks the role at its most protected point. A Pope can be politically difficult. A Pope can be stern, vain, theatrical, even manipulative. A Pope saying he does not believe in God creates a deeper rupture. It turns the title inward and asks whether the office can survive the private sentence inside the man.

Tommaso’s function matters. He wants to conduct and manage confession, to hold the procedure steady. Lenny gives him a claim that the procedure cannot easily domesticate. The open loop is clean: does Tommaso take it as provocation, joke, crisis, or truth? The episode does not settle that for him. It lets the question stand.

That is smart premiere construction. The hour begins by contesting whether Lenny is Pope and ends by contesting what that title means if belief itself is unstable. The contradiction map is the episode’s spine: Lenny wants conscience, identity, God, and confession expectations reconciled, then speaks in ways that make reconciliation harder. He insists on papal identity, accepts papal renaming, and detonates the core assumption beneath the office.

The scene also clarifies the score this hour earns. It is not a warm or emotionally generous pilot. It can be stiff, and some early dialogue arrives with the posture of a manifesto. But the architecture is confident. The episode knows the last line it wants to earn, and it builds toward it through naming, formality, political translation, and spiritual doubt.

## The Verdict

“Episode 1” is a strong, chilly premiere that turns papal authority into a live argument. Its best writing understands that names are actions: Lenny becomes Pope Pius XIII because the institution says so, then destabilizes the institution by speaking from inside it. The dense dialogue occasionally boxes out feeling, and a few ideological exchanges carry more design than pulse. Still, the hour has a fierce organizing idea and follows it with discipline. As a season opener, it plants the essential questions cleanly: whether Lenny’s papal identity can hold, whether Vatican power speaks through theology or around it, and whether Tommaso has heard a joke or a spiritual emergency.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 10
episode_reviews.review_body: The Young Pope Season 1 Episode 10 aired November 18, 2016 on Sky Atlantic as the season finale. Season 1 holds 79 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 87 critics; Metacritic 68; audience score on Rotten Tomatoes 87 percent. The RT consensus noted 'over-the-top melodrama with profane comedy.' The finale is the episode that justifies the preceding nine: the central mystery about Lenny's faith, his parents, and the nature of the show's theological argument resolves in a beach scene of such visual precision that critics who had found the season's pace punishing were most often won over here. Sorrentino's directorial instinct for the single crystalline image that retroactively earns an entire film's or series' indulgences - visible across his feature work - is at its most concentrated in the final scene. The 87-percent audience score, substantially above the critical score, reflects viewers willing to wait for exactly this payoff.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale resolves the season's central mystery about Lenny's faith and his parents with an image of such crystalline beauty that it retroactively earns the series' every indulgence. Sorrentino earns his epilogue.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final scene on the beach is the moment most often used to explain what the show is really about.
